article.title: Gen Z protests in Germany met with racial profiling and police harassment
article.author: Leon Wystrychowski
article.content: Even before the protests, held under the slogan “Gen Z Takes Charge” (“Gen Z regelt“), took place, politicians and mainstream media had been spreading scenarios of impending chaos. Around 120,000 people, mostly teenagers and young adults, took to the streets in more than 30 German cities to protest cuts to social welfare and compulsory military service, and to demand climate protection. Citing the mass protests in neighboring France – which, as usual, are portrayed in Germany’s dominant public discourse primarily as vandalism and rioting – the authorities and media also predicted a wave of violence for October 31, the day of the “Gen Z Takes Charge” demonstrations. Although this wave failed to materialize, clashes with the police did occur in several cities. Eyewitnesses report that, as a rule, it was the forces of the state that initiated the escalation. In Frankfurt, a major city, there was also some looting at a shopping mall following the protests, albeit on a limited scale. Whether, as in France, state agent provocateurs were directly involved is another question. In any case, those in power had deliberately whipped up expectations of precisely such incidents. And afterward, they were – predictably – made the centerpiece of media coverage and portrayed in exaggerated terms. “Migrant Milieu” under collective suspicion The “culprits” were quickly identified: Germany’s Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, of the conservative CDU/CSU, spoke of perpetrators from “the migrant milieu.” He received backing for this statement from fellow party members and the far-right AfD, as well as from conservative mainstream media. Words were quickly followed by action. In Frankfurt, the police have since launched a large-scale racial profiling campaign in the area surrounding the mall where the disturbances took place on October 31. After one week, the police proudly announced that they had carried out more than 1,000 checks. Those affected, however, are exclusively children, teenagers, and young adults – male and female – with dark skin and dark hair. Police officers arbitrarily stop these people as they walk around downtown, go shopping, eat, drink, or simply sit around with friends or family, or on their own, talking or making phone calls. They are ordered to show their IDs and open their bags. Police officers frequently even demand to search their victims’ cell phones. Young men standing side by side in a row against a wall, like dangerous hardened criminals caught red-handed, surrounded and cordoned off by several rows of police officers who also keep eyewitnesses at a distance, have now become an everyday sight in downtown Frankfurt. Racial profiling is officially prohibited in Germany. The term the police use to justify their actions is “checks without reasonable suspicion.” The fact that everyone affected belongs to the group Interior Minister Dobrindt has labeled “the migrant milieu,” and that the same individuals are sometimes stopped and searched two or even three times within a short period, is supposedly all just a coincidence. When asked about the racist checks, a Frankfurt police spokesperson cynically explained that the reason so many people of color were being stopped was that Frankfurt was “such a wonderfully diverse city.” Apparently, some of the spokesperson’s colleagues had not yet gotten the wording down. Deniz Avan, a left-wing local politician, told the left-wing daily junge Welt that a police officer he had confronted let something slip, inadvertently starting to say “Mi-” before cutting himself short and saying something about the “Gen Z” protests instead. Manufacturing a new enemy: “Islamo-Marxism” The campaign must be viewed in the context of militarization, the drive toward war against Russia, the associated policies of dismantling social protections and democratic rights, and the rise of the far-right AfD in Germany. Sharif Wali, an antifascist activist from Frankfurt, told BreakThrough News that there are three reasons behind the current racist campaign: young people who are currently becoming politicized are meant to be intimidated; racism directed against migrants and refugees is meant to be further stoked; and “the police state in Germany is meant to be further advanced.” The fact that the aim is to undermine political protest and resistance by marginalized groups is also evident in the way racism is being combined with an unmistakably anti-left agenda. Even before the “Gen Z Takes Charge” protests, Alexander Throm, the CDU/CSU’s spokesperson on domestic affairs in the German Bundestag, had warned of an “unholy alliance between left-wing extremist forces, sections of the migrant milieu, and criminals.” Immediately after the incidents in Frankfurt, Dobrindt had also blamed “left-wing groups and troublemakers from the migrant milieu,” before subsequently focusing on the latter. In doing so, the two leading conservative politicians are picking up a narrative that has been circulating among right-wing circles for some time and that recently entered the German mainstream following the Left Party’s election victory in the capital, Berlin : an alliance between “left-wing extremists” and “criminal migrants” – or, alternatively, “Islamists.” In France, right-wing politicians have been warning against “Islamo-Gauchisme” for several years. By now, this narrative has crossed over into Germany under the label “Islamo-Marxism.” The parallel with the Nazis’ notion of “Jewish Bolshevism” is obvious. It is equally clear that this modified image of the enemy fits all too neatly with the current political course pursued by those in power in Germany.
